title: NOTUS Contemporary Vocal Ensemble – Dominick DiOrio, director; David Conte, guest composer
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  Arvo Pärt: Cantus in Memory of Benjamin Britten (1977)David Conte: September Sun (2002)Britten: Hymn to St. Cecilia, Op. 27 (1942/66)James MacMillan: Seven Last Words from the Cross (1993)About the Artists  Recognized with The American Prizes in both Choral Composition (2014) and Choral Performance (2019, with NOTUS), Dominick DiOrio is an imaginative, enthusiastic, and energetic conductor and composer who has won widespread acclaim for his contributions to American music. He is professor of music and chair of the department in choral conducting at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he joined the faculty in 2012, and where he serves as director of NOTUS, IU's storied contemporary vocal ensemble, which has been invited to perform at regional, national, and international choral conferences, and with which he has released three commercial albums to critical acclaim. DiOrio also serves as artistic director and conductor of the Mendelssohn Chorus of Philadelphia, which he regularly prepares to sing with The Philadelphia Orchestra. DiOrio's love for contemporary music is reflected in his conducted repertoire, including works by such path-breaking composers as James MacMillan, Steve Reich, and Krzysztof Penderecki. Guest conducting appearances frequently feature his original compositions, including with the Choral Arts Society of Washington (SOLARIS), Houston Chamber Choir (I Am), Choral Arts Initiative (All Is), and the Young Naperville Singers (Young Today). As a composer, DiOrio has been hailed for a keenly intelligent, evocative style, which shows "a tour de force of inventive thinking and unique colour" (Gramophone). His over 70 published works have appeared at major venues around the world, including the Sydney Opera House, Lincoln Center, and Carnegie Hall. He composes for musicians of all ages and experiences and maintains an active writing schedule—completing over 70 commissions in the last decade. Recent commissioning partners include the San Francisco Gay Men's Chorus and the San Francisco Symphony, Children's Chorus of Washington, The Choral Arts Society of Washington, and "The President's Own" United States Marine Band. DiOrio earned a Doctor of Musical Arts degree in conducting from the Yale School of Music, as well as M.M.A. and M.M. degrees in conducting from Yale and a B.M. in composition summa cum laude from Ithaca College.David Conte has received commissions from the San Francisco, Dayton, Oakland, and Stockton Symphonies, the Lee Trio, the Ives Quartet, Chanticleer, the American Choral Directors Association Raymond Brock Commission, the American Guild of Organists, Sonoma City Opera and the Gerbode Foundation for his opera America Tropical. Since 1985, he has been professor of composition and since 2014 chair of the Composition Department at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Conte is the composer of over 150 works published by E. C. Schirmer Music Company. A Fulbright Scholar in Paris with Nadia Boulanger, where he was one of her last students, a Ralph Vaughan Williams Fellow, and an Aspen Music Festival Conducting Fellow, he earned a D.M.A. from Cornell University, where he studied with Karel Husa and Steven Stucky. In 1982, Conte worked with Aaron Copland preparing a study of the composer's manuscript sketches. He has taught at Cornell, Colgate University, the European-American Musical Alliance in Paris, the American Conservatory in Fontainebleau, France, and the Interlochen Center for the Arts. He cocomposed the score for the documentary Ballets Russes, shown at the Sundance and Toronto Film Festivals, and he composed the score for the PBS American Masters' documentary Orozco: Man of Fire. Conte's opera The Gift of the Magi has received over 40 productions in the United States, Canada, Europe, and Russia. In 2015, he was awarded the NATS Art Song Composition Award for his cycle American Death Ballads. In 2024, he was named Distinguished Composer of the Year by the American Guild of Organists. In 2025, two CD recordings of his work were released: Intimate Voices: Chamber Music of David Conte on the Pentatone label and a recording of his Sinfonietta with the Royal Philharmonic, recorded at Abbey Road Studios for the Orchid Classics label. His ballet based on Brokeback Mountain with choreographer Pontus Lidberg will premiere at the Guggenheim Theatre in New York in January. Next July, he will join the faculty of the Zodiac Academy near the Côte d'Azur, France. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Virtual Workshop: Polycentric Public Insurance and Climate Adaptation in Switzerland
description: As climate losses mount and private insurers retreat from vulnerable areas worldwide, the questions of who bears the risk and who acts on adaptation are becoming urgent. This talk presents findings from a study, conducted with Rebecca Bednarek and Konstantinos Chalkias, exploring how Switzerland's nineteen cantonal public-sector disaster insurers can provide compulsory, affordable, multiperil coverage without government subsidy while actively investing in prevention and mitigation. We propose that mechanisms familiar to Ostrom scholars — reciprocity, polycentricity, and self-regulation — can be extended to explain how government actors achieve what cross-sectoral partnerships often cannot, challenging the dominant view that the public sector should steer rather than row in addressing grand challenges.Eugenia Cacciatori is Reader (Senior Associate Professor) in Management at Bayes Business School, City St George's, University of London, researching technological and organizational innovation, professional knowledge, and the governance of complex societal challenges. Her recent research explores disaster insurance and AI adoption. Her work appears in journals such as the Academy of Management Journal, Organization Studies, and Research Policy.Paula Jarzabkowski is Professor of Strategic Management at the University of Queensland and Bayes Business School. A Fellow of the British Academy and of the Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia, she is a leading authority on the insurance protection gap and disaster resilience, and serves on the OECD High-Level Advisory Board for the Financial Management of Catastrophic Risk. She received the Academy of Management's Joanne Martin Trailblazer Award for her foundational work on Strategy-as-Practice.  —  This colloquium will start with 20 minutes of introductory remarks, followed by a discussion moderated by Greg Bloom, visiting scholar at the Ostrom Workshop and co-founder of the Climate Resilient Insurance Strategy Project (CRISP).

title: Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Arts, Community, and Memory
description:
Tickets on Sale Now!

September 30 – October 1, 2026
Two-day Event Cost: $37 ($35 + processing fees) / Student Discount $11 ($9 + processing fees)
This event spans 2 days at 3 venues. Wednesday, 9/30/26 from 9:00 AM – Midnight and Thursday, 10/1/26 from 9:00 AM – 6:30 PM.

Location

The iFell Gallery – 415 W. Fourth Street Bloomington, IN 47404
FAR Center for Contemporary Arts – 202 S Rogers St, Bloomington, IN 47404
Lotus Firebay – 105 S Rogers, Bloomington, IN 47404

Lotus is hosting a series of conversations about the crucial role that the arts play in building our communities and identities. Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Arts, Community, and Memory invites participants to consider how the arts help us make sense of the world around us, connect individual and collective experience, and understand the communities we share. 
This event is ticketed and open to the public. A detailed schedule of events and speakers is coming soon! 
What can you expect?
Conversation and dialogue are the beating hearts of this symposium. We have designed the program around a summer-long collaborative planning process with an emphasis on open and interactive session formats. On both days, the symposium offers an “UnConferencing” space for attendees and presenters to share questions, ideas, and feedback with one another. 
Symposium sessions will engage with themes such as: 

Creative Placemaking: Community Projects and Renovating Spaces
Storytelling and Our Shared Futures
Cultivating Intergenerational Collaboration in Arts and Culture
The Role of Global Arts Education in Our Communities
Creative Aging and Folk Arts Practice

To conclude the program we invite you to attend a keynote session with Michael Orlove (National Endowment for the Arts) and Dr. John Fenn III (American Folklife Center) 
Conversations in Bloom is intended to be both a forum for shared reflection and a space for professional development. Participants will discuss the opportunities and challenges of activating, celebrating, and preserving community culture through the arts, while also considering how personal, institutional, and communal histories are interwoven into the fabric of Bloomington’s cultural life. 
Who will be there?
Community partners for this event include: Cicada Cinema, Blueline Media, MDWST Fable, Black Vulture Project, Monroe County History Center, Exodus Refugee, Traditional Arts Indiana, Indiana University Arts and Humanities Council, Indiana University Center for the Study of Global Change, Indiana University Department of Folklore and Ethnomusicology…and most importantly YOU!

title: Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Art, Community, and Memory
location: I Fell Gallery and Studios; FAR Center for Contemporary Arts; Lotus Education and Arts Foundation, 105 S Rogers St, Bloomington, IN 47404
description: The essential goal of Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Art, Community, and Memory is to create a community forum for talking about community-making through the arts in Bloomington. The conceptual anchors of the program are arts, community, and memory, which serve as through-lines for thinking about the interplay between shared and individual experiences, work, and histories. Conversation and collaboration are the beating hearts of this program. All of the sessions and events were designed in collaboration with participating community partners over many months of intentional conversation and dialogue. Throughout the planning we pushed ourselves and our community partners to critically examine how our engagement with the arts helps us process the world around us and collectively produce a sense of community and animates memory in ways that help build towards shared futures. We look forward to continuing the conversation with you all.

title: ACES Horizon Talk: Book Talk with Dr. Eveline Washul
description: Dr. Eveline Washul will discuss her new book, High Lands, Pure Earth: Place Making, History, and Urban Transitions on the Tibetan Plateau (Cornell 2026). In the twenty-first century, China's accelerated urbanization has transformed the Tibetan Plateau. Yet Tibetan urban experiences continue to be profoundly shaped by senses of being in the world that long predate Tibet's subjugation into the modern Chinese nation-state. Combining novel analysis of Tibetan textual sources, ethnographic research, and Indigenous studies frameworks, Washul's book explores how Tibetans actively engage history, peoplehood, and place to build belonging and community even in urban spaces characterized by intense state-led development and assimilation.Please note that this event will be in person only. There will not be a Zoom or hybrid option. title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Anasthascia Boateng
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE
description: Bio  Anasthascia Boateng is a fourth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Anthropology. Her research examines how African international students in the United States navigate transnational care, resource sharing, and family obligations within diasporic communities. Drawing on economic anthropology, migration studies, and diaspora philanthropy, she examines the concept of "Black Tax," the expectation that individuals who achieve educational or economic mobility provide support to family and community members across borders. As an Ostrom research awardee and fellow, she investigates how informal institutions, collective action, and shared obligations shape students' everyday lives and contribute to broader conversations about governance, reciprocity, and social support in transnational settings.Title  "Black Tax": Diaspora Philanthropy or Burden? Governing Transnational Care among African International StudentsAbstract  This paper examines how African international students in the United States navigate the financial, emotional, and social obligations associated with Black tax the expectation that upwardly mobile individuals will provide material and social support to family members and communities across borders. Drawing on in-depth interviews with my interlocutors, the study investigates whether remittance is experienced as diaspora philanthropy, moral responsibility, collective care, or personal burden and under what conditions these meanings shift. The findings reveal that remittances operate simultaneously as expressions of love, kinship obligation, and collective investment, while also requiring students to reduce personal consumption, defer savings, and make difficult trade-offs between transnational responsibilities and daily life in the United States.About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems. title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas | Additional Films and Guests
description: When a pious television "reporter" Melvin P. Thorpe (Dom DeLuise) threatens to expose Miss Mona's (Dolly Parton) Texas brothel—the Chicken Ranch—to public scandal and close it down for good, she vows not to go down without a fight! With the help of her long-time secret sweetie Sheriff Ed Earl Dodd (Burt Reynolds), the two join together to keep the ranch open and, naturally, deepen their own romance along the way. Sing along through this extraordinary story about passion, scandal, community, and resistance! First premiering as a Broadway musical in 1978, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas film adaptation was a critical mixed bag upon its release, but the people loved it! The film brought in the biggest weekend box-office opening for a musical up to that point in time and was nominated for two Golden Globes: Best Motion Picture - Musical or Comedy and Best Actress in a Motion Picture or Comedy for Parton. Musical numbers include two of Parton's biggest hits: "Hard Candy Christmas" and "I Will Always Love You." [114 min; comedy, musical, romance; English]

Waitress
location: Indiana University Auditorium, 1211 E 7th St, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Meet Jenna, a waitress and expert pie maker who dreams of a way out of her small town and rocky marriage. Pouring her heart into her pies, she crafts desserts that mirror her topsy-turvy life such as “The Key (Lime) to Happiness Pie” and “Betrayed by My Eggs Pie.” When a baking contest in a nearby county (and a satisfying encounter with someone new) show Jenna a chance at a fresh start, she must find the courage to seize it. Change is on the menu, as long as Jenna can write her own perfectly personal recipe for happiness.
 Brought to life by a groundbreaking creative team, this hilarious hit Broadway musical features original music and lyrics by Grammy Award winner Sara Bareilles (“Brave,” “Love Song”), a book by acclaimed screenwriter Jessie Nelson (I Am Sam), original choreography by Lorin Latarro (Mrs. Doubtfire, Chess) and original direction by Tony Award winner Diane Paulus (1776, Jagged Little Pill, Pippin).
 “Waitress is a little slice of heaven!” says Entertainment Weekly, and is “sweet, sassy and passionate,” according to New York Magazine.
 “It’s an empowering musical of the highest order!” raves the Chicago Tribune. Don’t miss this uplifting and hilarious musical celebrating friendship, motherhood, and the magic of a well-made pie.
source: Visit Bloomington, Limestone Post, WFIU Community Calendar

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

Conversation and collaboration are the beating hearts of this program. We look forward to continuing the conversation with you all.

description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

title: McCalla Center Open Gallery Hours
location: McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, Indiana 47408
description: Outfitting IU Athletics: Hoosier Champions                  This exhibit showcases objects from IU's championship teams and athletes, connecting them to historic achievements in the Big Ten and the national stage. The items featured in the exhibit are from the IU Athletics Sports Memorabilia Collection and feature photos and videos provided by IU Athletics and Indiana University Archives.                Dates: November 14, 2025 - October 2026                                      By Their Own Hands: The Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame!          Founded in 1974 by the Culture and Ethnic Affairs Guild of the Oakland Museum of California, the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame began as a film lecture series and awards ceremony celebrating achievements of Black film industry figures. When that organization closed, they donated their materials to IU. In collaboration with the IU Black Film Center and Archive, this exhibit features objects from that collection, including founding documents, costumes, and handprints of inductees to the Hall of Fame.        Dates: September 2025 - December 2026                                      Capturing the Campus: T.C. Steele, Indiana University's First Artist in ResidenceCapturing the Campus pays tribute to renowned Hoosier artist T.C. Steele. The exhibit honors the century that has passed since his death by showcasing paintings form the artist's residency at IU and other relevant works. The exhibit will bring together Steele's landscapes from the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection and the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites' collection, allowing the holdings of these two collections to be viewed in one space.        Dates: April 17, 2026 - April 2026                   Multipurpose Room          Currently Featuring: The Gift of Collecting: Tina Jernigan          Jernigan was a passionate supporter of both Indiana University and the arts. She donated artworks to the IU Public Art and Cultural Heritage Collection upon her passing in 2024. With funding provided by Jernigan, Public Art professionally framed, hung, and preserved these pieces for this exhibit in the McCalla Building and for future installations on campus.         Dates: July 2026-July 2027

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

title: Honoring Charlotte Zietlow: A Memorial
location: Switchyard Pavilion,1601 S Rogers St, Bloomington, IN 47403, USA
description:
Please join us at Switchyard Pavilion on Thursday, October 1, from 3:00–5:00 PM, as we celebrate the life and legacy of Charlotte Zietlow (1934–2025).

Charlotte was a pioneering public servant, community advocate, and catalyst for change in Bloomington and Monroe County.

Over a career spanning five decades, she broke new ground as the first woman to serve as President of Bloomington City Council, and later as the first woman to lead the Monroe County Board of Commissioners.

A scholar of German and French literature, Charlotte brought a global perspective to everything she touched from civic leadership to her love of cookbooks and international culture.

She was also a devoted nonprofit leader, supporting organizations including Planned Parenthood and Middle Way House.

Charlotte left an indelible mark on our community and the many lives she touched. We hope you'll join us to honor her life and memory.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: The Importance of Voting for the LGBTQ+ Community
description: Make Your Voice Heard!                                  Join us for an evening of conversation, learning, and community as we explore the power of voting and civic engagement in shaping a more inclusive future for LGBTQ+ communities. Our guest speaker, Professor Steve Sanders, will share insights on the history of voting rights, the impact of collective action, and why participation in the 2026 election matters. Whether you're a first-time voter or a longtime advocate, you'll have the opportunity to ask questions, share perspectives, and connect with others who are passionate about making a difference.                                Steve Sanders is Associate Dean for Academic Affairs and Professor of Law in the Maurer School of Law at IU Bloomington. He holds additional appointments as an Adjunct Professor of Political Science and an affiliated faculty member with the Department of Gender Studies and the Kinsey Institute. Steve's primary teaching area is Constitutional Law, and his scholarship focuses on questions arising out of the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantees of equal protection and due process, with a special focus on issues affecting LGBTQ persons and same-sex couples. Steve developed and taught IU's first course on "Gay and Lesbian Politics" in 1996, chaired the committee that won approval for domestic partner benefits in 2001, and was a longtime member of the board of the IU LGBTQ+ Alumni Association. He has received a Leadership Award from Lambda Legal and is a three-time winner of the IU Trustees Teaching Award.Ready to take action? Register to vote! Visit www.indianavoters.in.gov to check your registration status or register to vote (you can also click on the "register" button below). Follow the LGBTQ+ Culture Center on QNews, Facebook, and Instagram for voter registration updates, election information, and important deadlines. The deadline to register to vote in Indiana is October 5, 2026.                                  Come learn, connect, and take the next step toward making your voice count. description: Attend an exclusive working dinner and strategy session for the Spring 2027 D.C. Global Policy Program. Don't just study global leadership. Put it into practice.  This intimate event is for students interested in the Hamilton Lugar Spring 2027 residency. It's a working dinner and a peek at what a global career actually feels like before you step into it.Why you should attend:Sit at the Table: Engage with leaders who have shaped global policy and international careers.    Alumni Insights: Hear from a panel of D.C. Program alumni regarding their on-the-ground experiences.    Professional Roadmap: Get a technical walkthrough of the Spring 2027 cycle, including the January 12 – May 2 residency dates.    The Logistics Bridge: Understand how the IU Capital Campus housing works and how the classes work for undergrads, grad, and PhD students.    The Strategy Session AgendaI. Biography: Ambassador & Professor Lee Feinstein  Ambassador Lee Feinstein is a Senior Managing Director and the President of McLarty Associates. He previously served as the U.S. Ambassador to the Republic of Poland and held senior positions at the Department of State, including Principal Deputy Director and a Member of the Policy Planning Staff. He was the Founding Dean of the Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies at Indiana University from 2014 to 2022. Ambassador Feinstein is a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and the American Academy of Diplomacy, and holds a JD from Georgetown University Law Center.   Can't make the full hour? title: Venezuela Talk with Dr. Yoletty Bracho at Redbud Books
description: Dr. Yoletty Bracho will examine neo-imperialism, neocolonialism, and grassroots resistance, drawing on the Venezuelan case.  Bracho is a researcher and adjunct professor of political science at the Université d'Avignon in southern France and an Impact+ postdoctoral fellow at the Université de Montréal. She holds a PhD in political sociology from the Université Lumière Lyon 2 and specializes in participatory public policy and left-wing activism in Venezuela. She is currently working on her book manuscript, Faire la Révolution dans l'État : participation et consolidation autoritaire au Venezuela, with Éditions Terres de feu.

title: University Orchestra – Thomas Wilkins, conductor
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire  R. Strauss: Wind Serenade in E-Flat Major, Op. 7 (1881)Elgar: String Serenade in E Minor, Op. 20 (1892)Coleridge-Taylor/Fletcher: Suite from "Hiawatha Ballet Music, Op. 82" (1912)Beethoven: Symphony No. 8 in F Major, Op. 93 (1812)About the ConductorThomas Wilkins is principal conductor of the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra, artistic partner for education and external engagement and Germeshausen Family and Youth Concerts Conductor Chair with the Boston Symphony Orchestra, and professor of music (conducting) at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he holds the Henry A. Upper Chair of Orchestral Conducting, established by the late Barbara and David Jacobs as a part of Indiana University's Matching the Promise Campaign. He is also music director laureate of the Omaha Symphony, where he was music director from 2005 through 2021, and principal guest conductor of the Virginia Symphony Orchestra. Past positions have included resident conductor of the Detroit Symphony and the Florida Orchestra (Tampa Bay) and associate conductor of the Richmond (Virginia) Symphony. He also has served on the music faculties of North Park University (Chicago), University of Tennessee in Chattanooga, and Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond. Devoted to promoting a life-long enthusiasm for music, Wilkins brings energy and commitment to audiences of all ages. He is hailed as a master at communicating and connecting with audiences. He has guest conducted orchestras throughout the United States. Wilkins' commitment to community has been demonstrated by his participation on several boards of directors, including the Greater Omaha Chamber of Commerce, the Charles Drew Health Center (Omaha), the Center Against Spouse Abuse in Tampa Bay, and the Museum of Fine Arts as well as the Academy Preparatory Center both in St. Petersburg, Florida. Currently, he serves as chairman of the board for the Raymond James Charitable Endowment Fund and as National Ambassador for the non-profit World Pediatric Project, headquartered in Richmond, Virginia, which provides children throughout Central America and the Caribbean with critical surgical and diagnostic care. A native of Norfolk, Virginia, Wilkins is a graduate of the Shenandoah Conservatory of Music and the New England Conservatory of Music (Boston). He and his wife, Sheri-Lee, are the proud parents of twin daughters, Erica and Nicole. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: CRRES Symposium: Venezuelan Politics in the Wake of Crisis
description: Venezuelan Politics in the Wake of CrisisFriday, October 2nd9:30a.m.-4:00p.m.Breakfast served at 9amHamilton Lugar School -Shreve AuditoriumFor Schedule: Center for Research Race & Ethnicity in Society's Event Page (https://crres.indiana.edu/events/venezuela-symposium.html)   Against the backdrop of political upheaval, foreign intervention, natural disaster, and long-standing infrastructure challenges, Venezuelan Politics in the Wake of Crisis will bring together scholars and a human rights advocate for an interdisciplinary examination of contemporary Venezuela.  The symposium will feature Verónica Zubillaga of the University of Illinois Chicago and Yoletty Bracho of Avignon University, joining in person; Magdalena López of the University of Notre Dame and the University Institute of Lisbon, joining virtually; and Venezuelan attorney and human rights advocate Venus Marina Faddoul Barrios, director of the NGO 100% Estrógeno, joining virtually from Spain.  Drawing on expertise in political participation, urban and state violence, cultural criticism, human rights, and gender justice, the panelists will examine how Venezuela's continuing crises have affected political life, civil society, migration and displacement, and regional relations. The program will also include a screening of 22 de mayo (1969) by Cine Urgente moderated by Dr. Noraeden Mora from the Department of Spanish and Portuguese.  Organized by the Center for Research on Race and Ethnicity in Society (CRRES), in collaboration with the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies (CLACS), the Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies (HLS), the Department of History, and the Department of Spanish and Portuguese. Meeting URL: https://iu.zoom.us/j/89320581931?pwd=UjTCinQOmrBAwblMTkz06GLsl3eOZ4.1

location: Musical Arts Center, 101 N Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, IN 47406
description:
White Shadows
Christian Claessens
Longtime Jacobs faculty member Christian Claessens teams up with the Jacobs Percussion Department to create this world premiere based on the last three movements of Steve Reich’s Sextet, employing marimbas, vibraphones, bass drums, and more. The eight dancers embody movement from pulsations to melodic patterns to rhythmic ambiguity.

Joseph Gramley, Conductor and Chamber Music Coach
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
Valse-Fantaisie
George Balanchine
Attended by their single partner, five ballerinas move in a whirl of perpetual motion to Mikhail Glinka’s waltzing rhythms. Although it was popularly called “the Melancholy Waltz,” this 1967 rendering is fast and light and was originally presented as the second section of Glinkiana, which featured former IU Distinguished Professor Violette Verdy in its New York City Ballet premiere.
George Balanchine, Choreographer
Kyra Nichols, Stager
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
Dignity in Restraint
Caili Quan
Born to a Chamorro Filipino family in Guam, Caili Quan created this punchy work on New York City Ballet dancers to Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12. Her love for “showing people the music” is on full display as she corresponds five major chords to the five core emotions of anger, fear, disgust, joy, and sadness.
Caili Quan, Choreographer
Andrea Yorita, Stager
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
World Premiere
James Whiteside
A principal dancer and choreographer with American Ballet Theatre, James Whiteside is also a pop music performer, model, drag queen, podcast host, and author. He brings his wildly eclectic style to Jacobs for several weeks as he creates his latest work, with the students of the Ballet Department.

title: Such Now the Necessity: The Declaration and Secession
location: IMU Federal Room, 900 E. 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
The symposium “Such Now the Necessity: The Declaration and Secession” is scheduled for 2 October, from 10:00am to 3:00pm, in the IMU Federal Room. The symposium considers the Declaration specifically as a secessionist document: how it functioned in the early United States, how it relates to broader theories of secession, and how it has been or might be used in other political contexts.
The Declaration of Independence is revered as the formative expression of American values. However, it was designed primarily as a legal and rhetorical address to the world—"to the opinions of mankind"—justifying a radical project: secession. The Declaration advances the two principal arguments that are familiar justifications used by secession movements today: an inherent right to self-government based on "consent of the governed," and "remedial secession" in response to "a long train of abuses." Given this founding DNA, why is the United States no longer a pro-secession advocate? What would it mean to take the Declaration’s arguments seriously today—both in America’s foreign relations and for America’s own territories (such as Puerto Rico) and the 50 states?

title: Happiness 2.0 mask workshop
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Throughout the fall semester, Indiana University undergraduate and high school students from the Bloomington community are invited to participate in the Happiness 2.0 Mask Workshops — an interactive experience that brings together science, art, and reflection on digital life.  The experience combines three components:an accessible discussion of current research on digital media and identity  a guided exploration of artworks in the Eskenazi Museum's galleries  a hands-on mask-making activity    Drawing inspiration from both the research discussion and the museum experience, participants will create a mask representing aspects of their own digital identity and experiences with digital media. Topics explored throughout the workshop include identity formation, online self-presentation, the relationship between online and offline selves, and well-being.

title: Lecture: "Lessons from a Rapid-Response Web-Archiving Effort" with Anna Kijas
location: Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies
description: Anna E. Kijas is Assistant Director of Digital Scholarship and Lilly Music Library at Tufts University. She co-founded Saving Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Online, an initiative focused on safeguarding and preserving the digital cultural heritage of Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War.  Anna's work is centered on principles of social justice, access, and sustainability in relation to digital humanities, historical (music) research, cultural heritage, and information studies. Her recent publications include a special issue, "Cultural Heritage in Crisis," for the journal Library Trends, a co-authored chapter, "Nimble Tents and Bunkers: The Role of Libraries in Rapid-Response DH," in The Routledge Companion to Libraries, Archives, and the Digital Humanities, a book entitled The Life and Music of Teresa Carreño (1853-1917): A Guide to Research, and open-access digital projects, including Documenting Teresa Carreño and Rebalancing the Music Canon. title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

location: Juniper Art Gallery, 615 West Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47404
description:

Special music by Elias Fisher, 6-7:30pm
Bound by Nature is a commissioned series of twenty original Art Nouveau-inspired illustrations created for the wedding of Erica Nadolkski and Jordan Evans.
Each poster celebrates a different insect personally selected by the bride, pairing it with native flora and elements of its natural habitat. Drawing inspiration from vintage natural history plates and the decorative compositions of the Art Nouveau movement, every illustration is framed by ornamental motifs unique to its featured species, incorporating elements from its life cycle, host plants, and surrounding ecosystem.
Originally designed as table markers for the couple’s wedding reception, the complete series extends beyond its ceremonial purpose as a celebration of transformation, growth, and the interconnectedness of nature. Like marriage itself, metamorphosis is a process of continual change. Reflected throughout the lives of the insects depicted in these illustrations.
Following the wedding, the collection will be exhibited at Juniper Gallery in October as a complete body of work with reproductions available.

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan "Meet the Artists" Reception
description: Join us for an evening with artists Qahar Behzad and Tiffany Black Behzad! Come check out their exhibition "In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan" and enjoy light refreshments from 5-8 pm.   In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.

title: An Evening With Cliff Cash
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: Cliff Cash hit his first open mic in 2011 at the age of 31. He didn’t miss a Thursday open mic after that for about a year. Within 2 years Cliff won Port City’s Top Comic, Comedy Central’s UpNext Regionals, Comedy Zone’s Almost Famous and landed himself on Sirius XM. In the years that followed, Cash racked up an impressive list of comedy credits and life scars. The highs and lows ranged from a divorce to a number one comedy album, from the death of his father to a Dry Bar Comedy special. Despite accolades like being a finalist for Standup NBC, having two albums reach number one, being on Laughs TV, Rooftop Comedy and more, Cliff was toiling away in the shadows of obscurity reluctant to take the traditional path of moving to New York or Los Angeles. Cash focused instead on honing his craft and building connections nationwide performing in nearly every state in the lower 48, touring for months at a time, living in a station wagon, camping, hiking and exploring between gigs. Many years he slept more nights under the stars than under a roof. He saw 45 of the nations 62 national parks and stumbled upon the passion of nature photography that he now sells as merch at his shows. Cliff lived in his old sprinter van for months at a time all over the U.S. and México. Finally Cliff gave in to the pressure of the social media path. He decided that 2025 would be the year he finally put his energy into his long neglected online presence. In less than 6 months, he’s grown his YouTube following from 280 subscribers to over 300,000 and the other apps have exploded in the same way. His first *real* comedy special THE LONG ROAD debuted to high praise from fans around the world, reached #1 on the iTunes comedy chart and has been viewed nearly 50 million times across clips and platforms. It is now available on apple, Amazon, tubi, Roku and more.

title: Tomorrow's Sentry
description:
***Tomorrow’s Sentry:* One forgotten trunk. One extraordinary life. One community’s untold story.**

When 102-year-old Bloomington resident Dot Weaver dies, she left behind fragments of a hidden history waiting to be discovered. Audiences are taken on an unforgettable journey though Monroe County’s controversial history — from the post Civil War era to today. Filled with celebrations, overdue realizations, and lessons for future generations, *Tomorrow’s Sentry* reminds us that today’s youth will become tomorrow’s guardians of history.

title: An Evening With Cliff Cash
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: Cliff Cash hit his first open mic in 2011 at the age of 31. He didn’t miss a Thursday open mic after that for about a year. Within 2 years Cliff won Port City’s Top Comic, Comedy Central’s UpNext Regionals, Comedy Zone’s Almost Famous and landed himself on Sirius XM. In the years that followed, Cash racked up an impressive list of comedy credits and life scars. The highs and lows ranged from a divorce to a number one comedy album, from the death of his father to a Dry Bar Comedy special. Despite accolades like being a finalist for Standup NBC, having two albums reach number one, being on Laughs TV, Rooftop Comedy and more, Cliff was toiling away in the shadows of obscurity reluctant to take the traditional path of moving to New York or Los Angeles. Cash focused instead on honing his craft and building connections nationwide performing in nearly every state in the lower 48, touring for months at a time, living in a station wagon, camping, hiking and exploring between gigs. Many years he slept more nights under the stars than under a roof. He saw 45 of the nations 62 national parks and stumbled upon the passion of nature photography that he now sells as merch at his shows. Cliff lived in his old sprinter van for months at a time all over the U.S. and México. Finally Cliff gave in to the pressure of the social media path. He decided that 2025 would be the year he finally put his energy into his long neglected online presence. In less than 6 months, he’s grown his YouTube following from 280 subscribers to over 300,000 and the other apps have exploded in the same way. His first *real* comedy special THE LONG ROAD debuted to high praise from fans around the world, reached #1 on the iTunes comedy chart and has been viewed nearly 50 million times across clips and platforms. It is now available on apple, Amazon, tubi, Roku and more.

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design
