title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Fall Ballet
location: Musical Arts Center, 101 N Eagleson Ave, Bloomington, IN 47406
description:
White Shadows
Christian Claessens
Longtime Jacobs faculty member Christian Claessens teams up with the Jacobs Percussion Department to create this world premiere based on the last three movements of Steve Reich’s Sextet, employing marimbas, vibraphones, bass drums, and more. The eight dancers embody movement from pulsations to melodic patterns to rhythmic ambiguity.
Christian Claessens, Choreographer
Joseph Gramley, Conductor and Chamber Music Coach
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
Valse-Fantaisie
George Balanchine
Attended by their single partner, five ballerinas move in a whirl of perpetual motion to Mikhail Glinka’s waltzing rhythms. Although it was popularly called “the Melancholy Waltz,” this 1967 rendering is fast and light and was originally presented as the second section of Glinkiana, which featured former IU Distinguished Professor Violette Verdy in its New York City Ballet premiere.
George Balanchine, Choreographer
Kyra Nichols, Stager
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
Dignity in Restraint
Caili Quan
Born to a Chamorro Filipino family in Guam, Caili Quan created this punchy work on New York City Ballet dancers to Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12. Her love for “showing people the music” is on full display as she corresponds five major chords to the five core emotions of anger, fear, disgust, joy, and sadness.
Caili Quan, Choreographer
Andrea Yorita, Stager
Blake Kile, Lighting Designer
World Premiere
James Whiteside
A principal dancer and choreographer with American Ballet Theatre, James Whiteside is also a pop music performer, model, drag queen, podcast host, and author. He brings his wildly eclectic style to Jacobs for several weeks as he creates his latest work, with the students of the Ballet Department.

title: Lotus Festival: All Inclusive Four-Day Pass
description:
**Lotus World Music & Arts Festival** showcases the exceptional talent of performing artists and musicians from around the globe. With a sense of discovery, exploration, and celebration, people of all ages, ethnicities, abilities, and backgrounds come to Bloomington, IN to experience Lotus over multiple days and venues. For over 30 years, this festival has been supported by countless community partners, sponsors, and volunteers.

20 Artists, 40 performances, over 4 days – Discover the music. Explore the arts. Celebrate world cultures. Experience Lotus – Indiana’s premiere music festival and annual celebration of music, arts, and culture.

Artist Line Up Coming Soon – Check back later!

The **All Inclusive Pass** will get you access to the Thursday night Opening Concert at the Buskirk-Chumley Theater, all concerts at all venues on Friday and Saturday, and the Sunday Closing Concert at the Buskirk-Chumley Theater. **September 30th is the last day to Purchase an All Inclusive Pass.**

**Wristbands:**

All Inclusive Wristbands will be available to pick up in the lobby of the Buskirk-Chumley theater starting Thursday the 1st at 5:30pm. Wristbands are not replaceable and must be worn all weekend to enjoy the festival. Wristbands not picked up on Thursday will be available at the Wristband Tents on the Friday and Saturday of the festival, when they open at 5:30pm. Please have your ID and ticket available at the time of pick up.

**Lotus Pins:**

The 2026 commemorative Lotus Pin will be available for pick up at a table in the lobby of the Buskirk-Chumley Theater on Sunday, October 4th when doors open for the Closing Concert. Please have your wristband and ID available at the time of pickup.

**Dates & Schedule**: The complete schedule will be available on the Lotus Fest website. A printed pamphlet will be available at arrival.

**10/1, 7pm – 9:30pm** Festival Opening Concert at Buskirk-Chumley Theater

**10/2, 6pm – 12am** Friday Showcase at Multiple Venues

**10/3, 12pm – 12am** Saturday Showcase at Multiple Venues

**10/4, 3pm – 5pm** Closing Concert at Buskirk-Chumley Theater

**Maps & Venues**: Maps of the festival will be available on the Lotus Fest website. A printed pamphlet will be available at arrival.

**Buskirk-Chumley Theater** – 114 E Kirkwood Ave.

**First Christian Church** – 205 E Kirkwood Ave.

**6th Street Stage** – 6th St between College Ave. and Walnut St.

**Arts Village Stage** – Kirkwood between College Ave. & Walnut St.

**The Bishop Bar** **(18+)** – 123 S. Walnut St.

**The BlockHouse Bar (21+)** – 205 S. College Ave.

Our family friendly venues include the Buskirk-Chumley Theater, Arts Village Stage, and Church venues. The outdoor tent can be louder and more boisterous, and occasionally, political statements are made. Parents should make their own decisions about which venues they choose to attend.

title: Future Tense 2026
location: Grunwald Gallery of Art, 1201 E. 7th Street, Fine Arts Building, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
The Grunwald Gallery of Art at Indiana University Bloomington partners with Surface Design Association to present "Future Tense 2026"—a national student exhibition juried by José Santiago Pérez. Since 2017, Surface Design Association (SDA) has invited students to submit work for the annual Juried Student Exhibition. The ninth iteration of this exhibition will be held at Indiana University’s Grunwald Gallery of Art in Bloomington, IN from August 25-October 31, 2026. Exhibiting artists are eligible for four awards recognizing excellence in artistic practice. 
"Future Tense” celebrates the creative work of student artists, designers, and makers working with, or inspired by fiber, or textile materials, or techniques. This exhibition offers a glimpse into the future of contemporary fibers by presenting the very best work being made by students in the field today.

title: Service of Witness to the Resurrection for Kim Gray
Tomorrow's Sentry
description:
Tomorrow’s Sentry: One forgotten trunk. One extraordinary life. One community’s untold story.

When 102-year-old Bloomington resident Dot Weaver dies, she leaves behind fragments of a hidden history waiting to be discovered. Audiences are taken on an unforgettable journey though Monroe County’s controversial history — from the post Civil War era to today. Filled with celebrations, overdue realizations, and lessons for future generations, Tomorrow’s Sentry reminds us that today’s youth will become tomorrow’s guardians of history.

title: Annual Grape Stomp Championship
location: Oliver Winery, 200 E. Winery Road, Bloomington, IN 47404
description:
Ever wanted to channel your inner Lucille Ball? Here's your chance! Grab three of your favorite people, roll up your pant legs, and get ready to stomp your way to glory. Teams of 4 will battle it out through two rounds of pure grape-crushing chaos, with the top 2 teams advancing to a winner-take-all championship round. The champions walk away with an epic prize: a hot air balloon ride!

Round 1 starts at 3:30pm, Round 2 at 4:30pm, and the championship round at 5pm. There's also a prize for Best Team Spirit, so feel free to bring some team pride.
Tickets for stompers are $25 per person or $100 for a full team of 4. You have to be 21 or older to participate. It includes a glass of wine plus a souvenir wine glass to take home, so you'll always remember the day you crushed it.

title: Maya, Give Me a Title | Adapt/Contruct, CINEKid's International Children's Film Series
location: IU Cinema, 1213 E. 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Maya and her dad—producer and filmmaker Michel Gondry—live in two different countries. In order to stay in touch, her dad asks her every evening, “Maya, give me a title.” Based on her answer, he creates a short animated reply in which Maya is the hero. In this charming and clever stop-motion animated adventure, the always innovative and whimsical Gondry brings to life a poetic and amusing journey that will have the little ones dreaming and the grown-ups smiling. [61 min; animation, adventure, family; French with English subtitles]
Before the screening, join us at 3pm in our lower lobby for a fun flipbook-making activity! Then, on October 24, come to the IU Sciences Library (located inside the Chemistry Building at 800 E. Kirkwood Ave.) anytime between 10am-4pm for a hands-on investigation into how things move. Show them your IU Cinema flipbook for a special sticker and goodie bag! All ages are invited to explore books on animation, physics, and other fun science-in-motion topics from the Education Library, then test your skills with mechanical puzzles from the Lilly Library's Slocum Puzzle Collection. Don't miss the chance to make your very own thaumatrope, a classic optical toy that brings still images to life! Plus, enjoy the button maker and take home a craft to remember your visit. It’s all part of ScienceFest 2026, a campus-wide celebration of science at Indiana University.

title: An Evening With Cliff Cash
location: The Comedy Attic, 123 S Walnut Street, Bloomington, IN
description: Cliff Cash hit his first open mic in 2011 at the age of 31. He didn’t miss a Thursday open mic after that for about a year. Within 2 years Cliff won Port City’s Top Comic, Comedy Central’s UpNext Regionals, Comedy Zone’s Almost Famous and landed himself on Sirius XM. In the years that followed, Cash racked up an impressive list of comedy credits and life scars. The highs and lows ranged from a divorce to a number one comedy album, from the death of his father to a Dry Bar Comedy special. Despite accolades like being a finalist for Standup NBC, having two albums reach number one, being on Laughs TV, Rooftop Comedy and more, Cliff was toiling away in the shadows of obscurity reluctant to take the traditional path of moving to New York or Los Angeles. Cash focused instead on honing his craft and building connections nationwide performing in nearly every state in the lower 48, touring for months at a time, living in a station wagon, camping, hiking and exploring between gigs. Many years he slept more nights under the stars than under a roof. He saw 45 of the nations 62 national parks and stumbled upon the passion of nature photography that he now sells as merch at his shows. Cliff lived in his old sprinter van for months at a time all over the U.S. and México. Finally Cliff gave in to the pressure of the social media path. He decided that 2025 would be the year he finally put his energy into his long neglected online presence. In less than 6 months, he’s grown his YouTube following from 280 subscribers to over 300,000 and the other apps have exploded in the same way. His first *real* comedy special THE LONG ROAD debuted to high praise from fans around the world, reached #1 on the iTunes comedy chart and has been viewed nearly 50 million times across clips and platforms. It is now available on apple, Amazon, tubi, Roku and more.

title: Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life w/ Q&A | IU Cinema Jon Vickers Scoring Award
location: IU Cinema, 1213 E. 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
In 1924, neophyte filmmakers Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, who would later co-direct King Kong (1933), hooked up with journalist and sometime-spy Marguerite Harrison and set off to film an adventure. They found excitement, danger, and unparalleled drama in the migration of the Bakhtiari tribe of Persia (now Iran). Twice a year, more than 50,000 people and half a million animals surmounted seemingly impossible obstacles to take their herds to pasture. The filmmakers captured unforgettable images of courage and determination as the Bakhtiari braved the raging and icy waters of the half-mile-wide Karun River. Although many documentary historians consider Grass second only to Nanook of the North, few people have actually ever seen this legendary film. This restored and full-length version will astonish today’s audiences with its beautiful photography and heart-stopping adventure. Presented with a recorded orchestral score by Patrick Holcomb that was world-premiered in IU Cinema's Virtual Screening Room in 2021. [71 min; documentary; silent film with intertitles]
Celebrating its first decade in 2026, the IU Cinema Vickers Scoring Award is named after IU Cinema’s founding director Jon Vickers; it is an IU Cinema-exclusive program produced in partnership with the Jacobs School of Music, and is generously endowed by former IU Trustee the Honorable P.A. Mack Jr.
A Q&A with composer Patrick Holcomb and IU Jacobs School of Music Professor Larry Groupé, moderated by IU Cinema Director Emeritus Jon Vickers, will follow the screening.
source: IU Cinema, IU Jacobs School of Music, Pillar Arts Community Calendar, Visit Bloomington

title: Sarah Jarosz: 10 Years of Undercurrent
location: Buskirk-Chumley Theater, 114 E Kirkwood Ave, Bloomington, Indiana 47408
description:
Presented by Buskirk-Chumley Theater
Originally from Wimberley, Texas, Sarah Jarosz is a six-time GRAMMY Award-winning singer, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist. Since her recorded debut in 2009, she has released seven solo albums and two albums with I’m With Her, her band with Sara Watkins and Aoife O’Donovan.
 In addition to her multiple GRAMMY, Americana Music Association, and Folk Alliance awards, her work has received widespread critical praise from publications including Rolling Stone, The New York Times, and USA Today. Jarosz has appeared three times on PBS’s legendary Austin City Limits television show and numerous times on A Prairie Home Companion, Live From Here, and the Grand Ole Opry. She is currently based in Nashville, Tennessee.
 Jordan Tice is an award-winning guitarist and songwriter described by the Fretboard Journal as “quite simply, one of our favorite acoustic guitarists performing today.” He has 7 projects to his name as a solo artist and 6 as a founding member of the string band, Hawktail.
 Equally virtuosic as a flatpicker and fingerstylist, and with a casual vocal style, Tice conjures ingredients from far-flung worlds with ease. His performances call upon the repertories of American and British Isles folk, bluegrass, blues, and pop-oriented songs, and though his earlier releases are instrumental in focus, he has been carefully honing his craft as a singer-songwriter in his most recent work. This includes his albums Motivational Speakeasy (produced by Kenneth Pattengale of The Milk Carton Kids and praised by NPR Music as “a really wonderful record”), Wild Rose of Morning (a collaboration with Andrew Marlin and Christian Sedelmyer), and Badlettsville.
 He has performed at festivals such as the Grey Fox Bluegrass Festival, Green Mountain Bluegrass and Roots, Red Wing Roots, Wintergrass Music Festival, and the Strawberry Music Festival and opened for artists like Watchhouse, I’m With Her, The Milk Carton Kids, and Madison Cunningham. In addition to his solo and collaborative work, he has performed and recorded as a sideman with Americana artists such as David Rawlings, Yola, Andrew Marlin, and Aoife O’Donovan.

Mortimer rushes to tell Abby and Martha before they stumble upon the body themselves, only to learn that the two old women aren’t just aware of the dead man in their parlor, they killed him! title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum.  Link to the artist's website:https://jamesnakagawa.com/en (https://jamesnakagawa.com/en)  FAR Center for Contemporary Arts:https://thefar.org/events/event/121689 (https://thefar.org/events/event/121689)

title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

description: $100 first-place prize in each category          Top 3 photos in each category will be displayed in GISB Atrium, Nov 16 - 20.          Winning photos will be permanently displayed in the Global and International Studies Building.    Who can enter?  Any HLS student who studied abroad Fall 2025, Spring 2026, Summer 2026 or Academic Year 2025-2026.  Photos must have been taken during your study abroad experience in your host country.Photo Submission CategoriesMost Picturesque: Capture a memorable landscape, cityscape, landmark, or other scene from your host country    Cultural Exchange: Share a moment that reflects meaningful engagement with or learning about your host community and culture    A Day in the Life: Show us a moment that captures what everyday life was like during your time abroad.    Photos that feature you and your IU spirit are encouraged!A few things to know before you submit:  Photos should tell the story of your study abroad experience while respectfully representing the people and places you encounteredMake sure people pictured are comfortable being photographed and having the photo publicly displayed  Photo featuring children or minors are not permitted  Do not submit photos featuring dangerous/prohibited activities, alcohol or drugs.   Avoid photos that stereotype, exploit, or disrespect people or cultures  Follow photography rules at religious, memorial, governmental, and culturally significant sites  Review the full photo ethics and contest guidelines (https://indiana-my.sharepoint.com/:w:/g/personal/ellcohen_iu_edu/IQCuZXL_BuC3SJQbjsVO7gvaAbUpX29xqtIFzjJ7JXaPBlY?e=6PUNCr)Photo Specifications  Submit your original, highest resolution photo (preferably 900 x 720 megapixels or greater)–not a screenshot or imagine downloaded from social media.  Low-resolution images may be removed from consideration.  Accepted file types: JPEG, PNGSubmit your photos here (https://forms.cloud.microsoft/pages/responsepage.aspx?id=NL4TEdGuAE2rS83QJRC-kUTyy7TLuDdAsrmI5CM6EKNURDVIOVhQTEk5SE1DTEVEQ0RQNzAwN0lXVC4u&route=shorturl) Meeting URL: https://forms.cloud.microsoft/r/qVJRcYhBnA

title: 33rd Annual Lotus World Music & Arts Festival
location: Multiple venues in downtown Bloomington, Bloomington, IN
description:
Indiana’s annual celebration of world music, arts, and culture. A four-day festival for people of all ages, ethnicities, abilities, and backgrounds that is supported by countless community partners, sponsors, and volunteers.
 Lotus showcases artists and groups from around the globe where you can expect unique opportunities and experiences that may broaden your worldview through the arts.
 Distinguished among other music festivals, Lotus Fest presents a non-hierarchical mix of performers and musicians highlighting the exceptional talent and unique characteristics of each artist.
 Join us for a weekend celebrating and exploring the diversity of the world’s cultures through music, art, food, dance, workshops, and fun for the whole family!

title: Annual Hilly Hundred Bicycle Tour
location: Routes take riders throughout the county, 601 Edgewood Drive, Ellettsville, IN 47429
description: A perennial winner of Bicycling Magazine and the League of American Bicyclists Best Biking in America Awards, the Hilly Hundred Weekend is a classic bicycling event designed for touring cyclists. If you like a bicycling challenge that includes entertainment and fellowship with more than 5,000 cyclists from over 40 states and several foreign countries, the Hilly is for you. This three day event (with two days of riding approximately 50 miles each day) is held in the scenic hills of southern Indiana. The challenging terrain is a wonderful mix of gently rolling country roads and breathtaking hills. Free food and live entertainment at each of three rest stops on both Saturday and Sunday

title: Tomorrow's Sentry
location: Waldron Arts Center, 122 S. Walnut St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description:
Tomorrow’s Sentry: One forgotten trunk. One extraordinary life. One community’s untold story.
When 102-year-old Bloomington resident Dot Weaver dies, she left behind fragments of a hidden history waiting to be discovered. Audiences are taken on an unforgettable journey though Monroe County’s controversial history — from the post Civil War era to today. Filled with celebrations, overdue realizations, and lessons for future generations, Tomorrow’s Sentry reminds us that today’s youth will become tomorrow’s guardians of history.

title: EXTENDED-LENGTH Explore Monroe Paddling Trip, Middlefork of Salt Creek (Monroe Lake)
location: Monroe Lake, Crooked Creek State Recreation Area (TC Steele / Crooked Creek Road, Nashville)
description:
EXTENDED-LENGTH Explore Monroe Paddling Trip at 12:30 p.m.

Registration required by October 1.Trip fee is $40 per person.Limited to 10 people. Restricted to ages 16 and up. All participants must be comfortable with paddling up to 12 miles in a single outing; this trip is not open to beginner-level paddlers.Bring your own canoe/kayak, or rent a sit-on-top kayak (weight limit: 275 pounds) for an additional $20.Location: Crooked Creek SRA (launch site) up the Middlefork of Salt Creek

Explore the quieter side of Monroe Lake during these guided paddling trips that journey through backwaters, wetlands, bays, and/or slow-moving streams. Trips highlight beautiful views, hidden wildlife, aquatic plants, and unique land features. Find your new favorite place to kayak! 2.5 hours 

BACKUP DATE is Friday, October 9 (same time). Please hold the backup date in your calendar, in case the trip must be rescheduled due to weather or instructor illness. Refunds will be offered only if the original AND backup dates are both cancelled.

This EXTENDED-LENGTH trip (about 5 hours, expected return around 5:30 p.m.) will head up the Middlefork of Salt Creek to the Elkinsville area. This is a particularly scenic portion of the Salt Creek Valley with a high likelihood of encountering bald eagles, beavers, and other wildlife. Due to the high-water levels experienced by the reservoir this summer, we may also encounter new logjams in the narrower sections of the creek – this trip is for those with an adventurous spirit!
 

REFUND/TRANSFER/CANCELLATION POLICY

Registrations are considered final and no refunds or date transfers are available, with limited exceptions. You may transfer a registration(s) to another person(s) by contacting Jill Vance at jvance@dnr.IN.gov from the same email used in your original registration. Provide the name(s) and email(s) of the person to whom you want to transfer the registration(s). Requests must be received at least 48 hours prior to the start of the workshop.In the event that the trip is cancelled by the instructor for weather, low registration, or instructor illness, registered participants may opt to transfer their registration to another Explore Monroe trip on a different date or receive a full refund. Weather Cancellation Policy: If only light rain is anticipated, the trip will likely proceed as scheduled. However, if there is a strong possibility (as determined by the instructor) of moderate to heavy rain, high winds, or thunder/lightning, the workshop will be cancelled for safety reasons. Any decision to cancel due to anticipated weather will be made at least 2 hours prior to the trip start time. In the event of a cancellation, an email notice will be sent to all registrants.Low Registration Policy: The trip may be cancelled, at the discretion of the instructor, if there are fewer than 3 people signed up by the registration deadline. If the trip is cancelled due to low registration, all participants will be notified within 24 hours of the close of registration.

title: War Paint: Women at War | Art and a Movie
description: Margy Kinmonth's feature documentary shines a light on the trailblazing role of women war artists, on the frontlines round the world, championing the female perspective on conflict through art. Culture breaks the taboo, crosses borders—tells the truth to power. Artists discussed include: Zhanna Kadyrova, Linda Kitson, Shirin Neshat, Rachel Reckitt, Dame Laura Knight, Lee Miller, Nina Berman, Marcelle Hanselaar, Jananne Al-Ani, Assil Diab, Doris Zinkeisen, Fiona Banner aka The Vanity Press, Maggi Hambling, Cornelia Parker, Dame Rachel Whiteread, Maya Lin, and including the work of Anne Desmet R.A., Samar Hussaini, and featuring Dame Penelope Lively, Charlotte Johnstone, and Ami Bouhassane. A cast of women contributors and crew makes this film a unique undertaking, telling vital truths in turbulent times. War Paint: Women at War is the third installment in Kinmonth's trilogy of films about how artists depict war, following the acclaimed Eric Ravilious: Drawn to War and War Art with Eddie Redmayne. [89 min; documentary, war; English]This program is presented in partnership with the Eskenazi Museum of Art. After the screening, continue the conversation at the Eskenazi Museum of Art with a special program led by museum photographer Shanti Knight. Register for this free event here.
source: Eskenazi Museum of Art, IU Cinema, Visit Bloomington

title: Sunday Live Music: CUADROS QUARTET
description:
Dave Bruker, John Valdez, Paul Kirk and Nate Johnson, together are Cuadros Quartet.
Dave Bruker likes composing tunes and playing jazz for the challenges and freedom that this genre of music allows.
John Valdez, has lived in Bloomington since 2003. He studied jazz drums at the Jacobs School of Music and has played with many of the local musicians both here and on the touring circuit.
Paul Kirk  has been playing the guitar for over 50 years and he especially likes to play jazz because of the shared musical interaction that happens when playing with other jazz musicians.
Nate Johnson is a musician and composer from Bloomington, Indiana. Skilled in multiple instruments and multiple styles of music, his saxophone can wail the blues or burn through bebop tunes, all with a soulful sense of cool.

title: It's On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop
description:
The It’s On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop is a 90-minute, audience-driven bystander intervention program that teaches students the skills needed to help in situations involving alcohol and drug use that could lead to a sexual assault. Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.  


It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.  


Instructions:  


Those who arrive more than 5 minutes after the start time will NOT be allowed into the session and will need to attend a different session 


If this is your assigned workshop but you cannot attend it in its entirety, please RSVP for a different workshop. 


If you have concerns about attending due to personal experiences or need to request accommodations, please contact the office at itsonus@iu.edu. 


All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all IU students and other members of the Indiana University community. 


Hosted by: Office for Sexual Violence Prevention and Victim Advocacy

Additional Information can be found at: https://beinvolved.indiana.edu/event/12491889

title: Arsenic and Old Lace [Live Theatre]
location: Brown County Playhouse, 70 S. Van Buren St, Nashville, IN, 47448, United States
description:
Drama critic Mortimer Brewster’s engagement announcement is upended when he discovers a corpse in his elderly aunts’ window seat. Mortimer rushes to tell Abby and Martha before they stumble upon the body themselves, only to learn that the two old women aren’t just aware of the dead man in their parlor, they killed him! Between his aunts’ penchant for poisoning wine, a brother who thinks he’s Teddy Roosevelt, and another brother using plastic surgery to hide from the police – not to mention Mortimer’s own hesitancy about marriage – it’ll be a miracle if Mortimer makes it to his wedding. Arsenic and Old Lace is a classic dark comedy about the only thing more deadly than poison: family.

title: Art & a Movie at the Eskenazi Museum: Women Photographers with Shanti Knight
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: 3:00-3:30 p.m. Martin Commons, 2nd floor  Knight will present a talk exploring the contributions of women photographers throughout history. Drawing inspiration from themes raised in War Paint, the lecture will highlight the important role women have played behind the camera, often in the face of significant barriers, as well as women's current challenges and opportunities within the profession.3:30-4:00 p.m. "Ask Me Anything" conversation with Knight. She will share insights from her work as the Eskenazi Museum of Art's photographer and reflect on her experiences as a full-time professional photographer.  After the program, guests will receive a list featuring works by women photographers in the museum's collection and in The Photographic Reflex. From 4:00-5:00 p.m., visitors are invited to explore the museum independently and spend time with these artworks.Bio:Shanti Knight has been the photographer at Eskenazi Museum of Art since 2019. She began working in the field as a teenager, growing up in her father's photography business and starting her independent practice in her 20s. She earned her Bachelor of Arts in Journalism with a Second Concentration in Fine Arts from Indiana University in 2011. She launched her career in New York City with an internship at Glamour magazine. In the years following, she has assisted, shot for, and received direct training and mentorship from more than 30 different professional photographers, mostly high-end professionals in New York City and Chicago with a variety of specialties, including, but not limited to, wedding, editorial, fashion, and commercial work, and she has served clients from coast to coast.

title: Baroque Orchestra – Ingrid Matthews, director
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!Repertoire to be announcedAbout the DirectorIngrid Matthews is professor of practice in historical performance (baroque violin) at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. A graduate of IU, where she studied with Josef Gingold and Stanley Ritchie, Matthews is one of today's most respected baroque violinists. Since winning first prize in the Erwin Bodky International Competition for Early Music in 1989, she has appeared as soloist, guest director, chamber musician, and concertmaster with leading early music ensembles, including the New York Collegium, Australian Brandenburg Orchestra, Boston Early Music Festival Orchestra, Ars Lyrica (Houston), Tafelmusik Baroque Orchestra (Toronto), Musica Pacifica (San Francisco), and many others. Matthews cofounded the Seattle Baroque Orchestra in 1994 and served as its music director until 2013. Matthews has won high critical acclaim for her extensive discography. Her recording J. S. Bach: Complete Sonatas and Partitas for Violin was named "top recommendation for this music … on either period or modern instruments" by American Record Guide. She also plays jazz and swing styles and is active as a visual artist. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Ostrom Workshop | Colloquium: Andrew Flachs
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE
description: Bio  Dr. Andrew Flachs researches food and agriculture systems, exploring genetically modified crops, heirloom seeds, and our own microbiomes. An associate professor of anthropology at Purdue University, his work among farmers in North America, the Balkans, and South India investigates ecological knowledge and technological change in agricultural systems. Funded by institutions including the National Geographic Society, the American Institute of Indian Studies, the National Science Foundation, and the Social Science Research Council, Andrew's work has resulted in over three dozen peer-reviewed publications, five books, and public-facing work in venues including Sapiens, Civil Eats, Salon, and the National Geographic magazine. Outside of academia, he is an avid cook, cyclist, embarrassing dad to three children, and musician who has performed in New York City, St. Louis, Asheville, and the San Francisco Bay Area.Title  Agriculture as social reproduction: Identifying mutually reinforcing diversity in small farmsAbstract  Social reproduction theory illuminates how the material and social fabrics of society are formed, recognizing value that is otherwise externalized in capitalist accounting. While it offers a robust vocabulary for describing how class, identity, and other ways of being in society are formed, this approach rarely places lived experiences within larger political ecologies. In this talk, I consider both how social reproduction reproduces socioeconomic conditions and class relations, as well as how this work reproduces physical landscapes that generate future possibilities for organizing life. Agriculture is a particularly illuminating case to describe how work reproduces social relationships while continually creating a landscape in which diverse life can thrive (or suffer). Across India, Bosnia, and the US Midwest, three different sorts of farms with three very different regional histories, I explore the role of commons and public infrastructure in creating diverse ecologies that sustain diverse social relations that sustain diverse economies.About the Colloquium SeriesEach Monday throughout the academic year, speakers share and discuss cutting edge research echoing the themes of the Ostrom Workshop's research program. Topics range from the governance of space, cybersecurity, and data management, to the environment, political economy, and sustainable food science. Presenters are from IU and around the world. Join us at the workshop or over Zoom to learn how the Ostrom legacy is evolving today. For more information, see ourwebsite (https://ostromworkshop.indiana.edu/index.html). title: EASC Colloquium: The Courtesan's Memory, Voice, and Late Ming Drama - Peng Xu
description: Peng Xu's The Courtesan's Memory, Voice, and Late Ming Drama argues that courtesans of the era played an active role in the theater and their impact manifested in Chinese literary history, albeit concealed or erased. In the late Ming dynasty (1368–1644), theater was dominated by male performers with professional actresses largely absent from the stage, unlike in the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368), where women performed without restriction in theater troupes. Despite the prevailing assumption that women played no part in the theatrical movement, The Courtesan's Memory, Voice, and Late Ming Drama illuminates how courtesans, as serious theater artists and playwrights, left a significant mark on the male-dominated dramatic and literary landscapes. This study profoundly remaps the textbook narratives of gender bias, challenges modern prejudices prevalent in the literary history of Chinese drama, and reveals how theatrical conditions and writing styles shifted to accommodate courtesan performances.  Utilizing a wide range of sources such as scripts, city guides, biographies, diaries, letters, wood-block illustrations, and paintings, this study distinguishes itself from earlier studies of Chinese courtesans by not thematizing courtesans for their allegorical values, but rather pinpointing their agency in shaping the features of Chinese theater and recognizing courtesans as a source of creativity and development in the medium. Xu's focus on courtesan performance culture allows for fresh readings of canonical Chinese plays, opening up new ways of understanding the history of Chinese drama written by women, thus deviating from standard historiography based solely on the writings of men.About the author: Peng Xu received her Ph.D. from the University of Chicago and was a postdoctoral fellow at UC Berkeley. Currently Associate Professor at ShanghaiTech University, she has held academic appointments at institutions across the U.S. and Asia. She actively promote cross-disciplinary and transnational dialogues in Chinese literary and performance studies, with a particular emphasis on the agency of actresses and women poets. She has published in leading journals including Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies, Late Imperial China, T'oung Pao, CLEAR: Chinese Literature, Essays, and Reviews, and Ars Orientalis. Her research-related activities have been funded by the Kyujanggak Institute at Seoul National University (2021), Fulbright American Scholar program (2020), ACLS/Henry-Luce Foundation (2018), among others.  An award-winning scholar-performer specializing in Kunqu and Peking Opera, Dr. Xu integrates scholarship and stage practice, bringing historical insight and aesthetic precision into every performance.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

She has worked at YouTube and Pandora and, most recently, has spent five years at Spotify as the Head of Editorial for Nashville, where she led the team that covers rock and alternative, country, and Christian and gospel music programming. title: Tom Walsh Jazz Ensemble
description: Enjoy this performance from almost anywhere in the world viaLIVE@jacobs!About the DirectorTom Walsh is Robert J. Waller Sr. and Robert J. Waller Jr. Professor of Music (saxophone) and chair of the Jazz Studies Department at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. An active performer of jazz and classical music, he has presented concerts and workshops in South Africa, China, Brazil, Japan, Azerbaijan, Costa Rica, in Europe, and across the United States. He is the co-author of the fifth edition of Creative Jazz Improvisation (2022) with Scott Reeves. His beginning improvisation book Jazz Master Teaches You to Improvise was published by Shanghai Music Publishing House in 2019. Recent recordings include The Pandemic Sessions by the IU jazz faculty, Luke Gillespie's Moving Mists, Basically Baker, Vol. 2, with the Buselli-Wallarab Jazz Orchestra (Patois), and Mike Hackett's New Point of View (Summit). Premiere performances include Scott Jones's concert band arrangement of Russell Peck's The Upward Stream, Chris Rutkowski's Concerto for Alto Saxophone and Wind Ensemble, and David Baker's Concerto for Alto Saxophone and Orchestra. His latest solo CD release is Intersections (Arizona University Recordings). Earlier solo CDs include New Life (RIAX) and Shaking the Pumpkin (RIAX). Other releases include the David Baker Concerto on Paul Freeman Introduces David Baker, Vol. XII (Albany), Basically Baker with the Buselli/Wallarab Jazz Orchestra (Patois), and Sky Scrapings: Saxophone Music of Don Freund (AUR). Walsh is a Yamaha Performing Artist and a Vandoren Artist. He taught at the Jamey Aebersold Summer Jazz Workshops from 1991 to 2019. He co-leads the IU Summer Saxophone Academy with Otis Murphy and is co-director of the College Audition Preparation Workshop. Walsh earned degrees in Saxophone Performance and Jazz Studies from Indiana University, where his principal teachers were distinguished classical saxophonist Eugene Rousseau and renowned jazz educator David Baker. His other influential teachers include Mike Tracy, Pat LaBarbera, Jerry Coker, and David Liebman. Meeting URL: https://liveatjacobs.music.indiana.edu/

title: Osamu James Nakagawa: TRACE | Exhibition
location: FAR Center for Contemporary Arts, 202 S. Rogers St., Bloomington, IN 47404
description: Opening reception and artist talk: Friday, September 4, 58 pm  Nakagawa combines photographs taken at the sites of Japanese-American incarceration camps with photograms of found objects and rubbings of the memorials.  Using diptychs, Nakagawa pairs the past and the present, flattening the boundaries between them. TRACE seeks to reveal what can't be seen anymore, things that happened eighty years ago and have been quietly buried. Through a direct and immersive process, using actual objects and surfaces from the sites, Nakagawa unearths this history of forced incarceration.About the artist:  Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City in 1962, raised in Tokyo, and then returned to the US at the age of 15. He is the Distinguished Professor and the Ruth N. Halls Professor of Photography at Indiana University. Nakagawa is a recipient of the 2010 Guggenheim Fellowship, the 2010 Higashikawa New Photographer of the Year and 2015 Sagamihara Photographer of the Year in Japan.  Nakagawa's work has been exhibited internationally, selected solo exhibitions include PGI, Tokyo; Kyoto University of the Arts; Sepia EYE, New York; Sakima Art Museum, Okinawa, Japan; and others. Group shows include "A Shared Elegy" with Emmet Gowin and Elijah Gowin; and "After Photoshop" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. His work is included in numerous public collections, including George Eastman Museum and the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum. title: Story: Sajik Kim exhibition
description: Artist Talk: Friday, September 11, 12–1 pm, Shreve Auditorium-Global and International Studies Building (355 N. Eagleson Avenue)Opening reception: Friday, September 11, 6–8 pm, Grunwald GalleryArtist Performance: Friday, September 11, 7 pm, Grunwald GalleryCo-curated by Osamu James Nakagawa (Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Photography) and Linda Tien (Director of the Grunwald Gallery), photography exhibition STORY is a creation myth drawn from the lived experience of Zainichi artist Sajik Kim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national. Infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance, STORY explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity.Directed by Kim herself,STORYposes the question: What is homeland? Every nation and people possess a creation myth that narrates the beginning of their community and sustains their collective identity. Yet, forZainichi artistKim, born and raised in Japan as a third-generation Korean national, there was a persistent sense of not being able to fully embody a fixed ethnic identity. From this position, Kim attempts to weave a personal "creation myth" drawn from her lived experience.In developing this series, Kim conducted research within Japan, incorporating elements from everyday life—such as food, clothing, housing, education, and festivals as well as encounters with people and historical events.STORYthus explores how one might establish a sense of self and live with rootedness amid the constant flux of identity. Furthermore, it seeks to resonate with and offer insight to those who, in an increasingly complex world, must navigate similarly unstable identities.Employing the methodology of staged photography, theSTORYseries is orchestrated through comprehensive direction—including lighting, makeup, costume, and posing. While photographic in form, the works are simultaneously infused with theatrical elements and embodied performance.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Be a Part of the"Day in My Life"Series
Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Lunch and Moderated Q&A with Carol Anderson
description: Carol Anderson will join Randal Jelks (https://aaads.indiana.edu/about/faculty/jelks-randal.html) (Ruth N. Halls Professor of African American and African Diaspora Studies) for a conversation about her research and career as a public writer, reflecting on the importance of intersecting the arts and humanities with civic engagement. The discussion will be followed by an audience Q&A, and this event will be limited to the first 60 people to register.  Professor Anderson will also give a public lecture, "One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression is Destroying Our Democracy," at the Buskirk-Chumley Theater on Tuesday, October 6 at 7pm. The event is free, but ticketed. Tickets are available at the BCT's website (https://buskirkchumley.org/events/one-person-no-vote-a-lecture-and-q-a-with-carol-anderson-october-6-2026/) and box office.  Carol Anderson is the Robert W. Woodruff Professor of African American Studies at Emory University. She is the author of several bestselling books including: The Second: Race and Guns in a Fatally Unequal America (2020); One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression is Destroying Our Democracy (2018), which was long-listed for the National Book Award in Non-Fiction; and the critically-acclaimed White Rage: The Unspoken Truth of Our Racial Divide (2016), which won the 2016 National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism, was a New York Times Editor's Pick, and was listed on the Zora List of 100 Best Books by Black Women Authors since 1850.  Professor Anderson is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the American Philosophical Society, and a recipient of the Ella Baker Lifetime Achievement Award from the Hurston/Wright Foundation. Her groundbreaking research has been supported by fellowships from the American Council of Learned Societies, the Ford Foundation, National Humanities Center, Harvard University, and the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History.  This event is presented with generous support from the College of Arts & Sciences and the Ruth N. Halls Humanities Fund.

title: Treasures of the Silk Road
location: McCalla Center, McCalla Center, 525 E. 9th Street, Bloomington, IN 47408
description:
The McCalla Center, in collaboration with musician and scholar Shahyar Daneshgar, celebrates the opening of its new exhibition Treasures of the Silk Road on Friday, September 25th, 4:00 pm-6:00 pm EDT.
The exhibit features over 70 musical instruments from the Pastel-Daneshgar musical instrument collection, with a focus on strings, flutes, and percussion from across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Crafted from wood, snakeskin, horsehair, lambskin, camel bone, and other unique materials, these instruments provide a compelling history of cultural and artistic exchanges that have led to the myriad musical sounds and styles that permeate the world today. The opening event will feature remarks from the collection owner, Shahyar Daneshgar, and will feature musical clips provided by the Lotus World Music & Arts Festival.
Shahyar Daneshgar is a lifelong musician, scholar, and cultural ambassador whose passion for traditional music has shaped more than three decades of collecting, teaching, and performing. Born into a large musical family, he studied at the Tehran Conservatory of Music before pursuing academic work in Germany and later at Indiana University, where he earned his Ph.D. in Central Eurasian Studies in 1995. He taught at Indiana University until his retirement in 2024. He is founder and director of the Bloomington Silk Road Ensemble.
The exhibition is free and runs from September 25, 2026, to September 2027.
The mission of the McCalla Center is to provide accessible exhibition and educational experiences, creating opportunities for students, faculty, and the community to engage with collections, IU-generated creative activity, and community projects in meaningful and innovative ways.

title: Burke Lecture Series: Dr. Huey Copeland
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: In this lecture drawn from his new book project, Huey Copeland considers how disciplinary structures differently value and tend towards the racialized historicity of the aesthetic, above all to those blackened beings whose everywhere present yet suppressed exertions continue to provide the preconditions for the emergence of the visual, the modern world, and the work of artists on the engendering of both.  Dr. Huey Copeland is the Andrew W. Mellon Chair and Professor of Modern Art and Black Study at the Universtiy of Pittsburgh. Copeland's work interrogates African/Diasporic, American and European artistic praxis from the late 18th-century to the present with an emphasis on articulations of blackness in the Western visual field. In his interdisciplinary research, Copeland focuses on the intersections of race and gender, subject and object, the aesthetic and its others from a black feminist perspective that reveals the biases and elisions of the discipline. Rather than assume the redemptive power of art, he aims to push history against the grain in exploring the constitutive relationship between the capture of black life and the production of cultural property in the modern transatlantic world.     Lecture will be held until 5 pm followed by questions. Reception to follow.Sponsored by the Robert E. & Avis Tarrant Burke Lecture Fund.

title: Fall 2026 CLACS Faculty Research Symposium with Eduardo Herrera
description: CLACS welcomes Eduardo Herrera (Folklore and Ethnomusicology) for the first CLACS Faculty Research presentation of the Fall 2026 semester. Join us as he presents:Sounds of the World Cup: Fan Atmospheres, Collective Affect, and Sonic PracticesAbstract: Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork conducted during the 2026 FIFA Men's World Cup in Buenos Aires, this presentation examines how sound, collective memory, and national narratives shaped Argentine experiences of the final stages of the tournament. Focusing on the contrasting atmospheres surrounding Argentina's semifinal against England and final against Spain, I consider how the historical memory of the Malvinas/Falklands War, comparisons between Lionel Messi and Diego Maradona, and newly circulating World Cup chants intensified the affective stakes of watching and supporting the national team. Photographs, field recordings, and video illustrate how collective sounding and embodied participation transformed World Cup spectatorship into a powerful site for experiencing national belonging, historical memory, anticipation, and defeat.

Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.  


It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.  


Instructions:  


Those who arrive more than 5 minutes after the start time will NOT be allowed into the session and will need to attend a different session

If you have concerns about attending due to personal experiences or need to request accommodations, please contact the office at itsonus@iu.edu.

title: One Person, No Vote: A Lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson
description:
**One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression is Destroying Our Democracy, a lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson**

Carol Anderson is the Robert W. Woodruff Professor of African American Studies at Emory University. She is the author of several bestselling books including: *The Second: Race and Guns in a Fatally Unequal America* (2020); *One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy* (2018), which was long-listed for the National Book Award in Non-Fiction; and the critically-acclaimed *White Rage: The Unspoken Truth of our Racial Divide* (2016), which won the 2016 National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism and was also a *New York Times* Bestseller, a *New York Times* Editor’s Pick, and listed on the Zora List of 100 Best Books by Black Woman Authors since 1850. Professor Anderson is also the author of *Eyes Off the Prize: The United Nations and the African-American Struggle for Human Rights*, *1944-1955* (Cambridge University Press), which was awarded both the Gustavus Myers and Myrna Bernath Book Awards. Her book *Bourgeois Radicals: The NAACP and the Struggle for Colonial Liberation*,*1941-1960* was published by Cambridge in 2014.

She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the American Philosophical Society, and a recipient of The Ella Baker Lifetime Achievement Award from The Hurston/Wright Foundation.

Her ground-breaking research has, additionally, been supported by fellowships from the American Council of Learned Societies, the Ford Foundation, National Humanities Center, Harvard University, and the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History.

The College Arts + Humanities Institute is pleased to present this event with support from the Ruth N. Halls Humanities Fund and the College of Arts & Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington.

CART captioning and ASL interpretation will be provided for the event. There will be a Q&A after the event. Tickets limited to 4 per person. Groups may contact cahi@iu.edu to request a larger order.

title: Mangrove School + Makongo/Caterpillars w/Q&A | For All the Children
description: Mangrove School(Filipa César and Sónia Vaz Borges, Guinea Bissau, 2022): During the anticolonial struggle against Portuguese occupation, the free schools in Guinea Bissau moved deep into the jungle and found the mangroves. The schools were fashioned on the interwoven branches and roots. The directors film the mangroves as an infrastructure with a networked architecture, as the locus of transmission, of radical education, attentive to the memory of the struggles. The mangrove's branches are powerful and encourage networks, collectives, and horizontality. [35 min; documentary; Portuguese with English subtitles]Makongo/Caterpillars(Elvis Sabin Ngaïbino, Central African Republic, 2020): Albert and André strive to create a school in their forest community in equatorial Central African Republic. As the only secondary school graduates in their village, they teach local children while relying on the annual makongo (caterpillar) harvest to fund their project. This vivid ethnographic portrait offers no embellishment, no narration, and no added music. The direct cinema approach is remarkably sensitive, attuned to the sounds of animals, the rain forest, and the daily life of the men and their families. [73 min; documentary; Sango and French with English subtitles]A Q&A will follow the screening.
source: IU Cinema, IU Hamilton Lugar School, Visit Bloomington

title: An Evening with Sutton Foster
location: Indiana University Auditorium, 1211 E 7th St, Bloomington, IN 47405
description:
Sutton Foster is a two-time Tony Award-winning actress, singer, and dancer widely recognized as one of Broadway’s leading performers. For her Bloomington performance, she will be joined onstage by IU dance and choral students along with local K-12 performers for what promises to be a special evening.
 Foster most recently starred as Princess Winnifred in Once Upon a Mattress  during its acclaimed Broadway revival. Prior, she starred as Mrs. Lovett in the Tony Award-winning Broadway revival of  Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street , as well as Marian Paroo in the 2022 Broadway revival of  The Music Man , earning her seventh Tony Award nomination.
 She first rose to prominence originating the title role in Broadway’s Thoroughly Modern Millie , earning her first Tony Award, and later won her second for  Anything Goes . Her extensive stage credits include  The Drowsy Chaperone ,  Shrek the Musical ,  Young Frankenstein ,  Violet , and  Sweet Charity. 
 On screen, Foster starred in TV Land’s Younger  and appeared in  Bunheads, Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life , and the final season of  The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel . As a solo artist, she has toured the country with stops at Carnegie Hall, Feinstein’s, Lincoln Center’s American Songbook series, and many others. Foster holds an honorary doctorate from Ball State University, where she also teaches.
